paragraphs.heading: The warm phase
paragraphs.text: The El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, is a worldwide climate pattern that shows up as rising and falling sea surface temperatures across the tropical Pacific Ocean. El Niño is its warming phase, and La Niña is its cooling phase. The Pacific moves between El Niño, La Niña and a neutral state in an irregular way, roughly every two to seven years, and each event has its own strength. ENSO tends to be strongest during the northern hemisphere winter, though its effects in a given region may peak at other times.

paragraphs.heading: What normal looks like
paragraphs.text: To see what El Niño changes, start with an ordinary year. Strong trade winds near the equator push water away from the eastern Pacific and pile it up in the west. The sea northeast of Australia averages around 28–30 °C, while the sea off the west coast of South America is nearer 20 °C. The pile-up is real enough that sea level near Indonesia usually sits about 0.5 m higher than near Peru. In the east, cooler water from the deep ocean rises to take the place of the surface water pushed away, a process called upwelling.

paragraphs.heading: How an El Niño builds
paragraphs.text: A central part of the machinery is the Bjerknes feedback, which takes its name from Jacob Bjerknes and dates to 1969. Changes in the air alter sea temperatures, and those sea changes alter the winds again, so each pushes the other further. When the easterly trade winds weaken, warm surface water surges east and upwelling along the equator slows. The sea surface warms, which is what we call El Niño, and the Walker circulation, a loop of air in the atmosphere turning over from east to west, weakens, so the trade winds drop even more. In the end the warm water in the western Pacific runs low enough that conditions return to normal, though the exact causes of the cycle are still being studied.

paragraphs.heading: The air pressure side
paragraphs.text: The ocean changes come with changes in the air above it, including wind, surface air pressure and cloud cover. During El Niño, air pressure is unusually high over Indonesia and the western Pacific and unusually low over the eastern Pacific. This pattern is called the negative phase of the Southern Oscillation. Today the name El Niño means the warm and negative phase of the whole ENSO pattern.

paragraphs.heading: Effects around the world
paragraphs.text: El Niño upsets normal weather patterns, bringing intense storms to some places and drought to others. Each event lifts the global average surface temperature for a short time, about a year. So how often El Niño comes compared with La Niña can tilt global temperature trends over spans of around ten years. The hardest-hit countries are developing nations on the edge of the Pacific that rely on farming and fishing. How climate change will alter ENSO is uncertain, but it does make the droughts and floods linked to ENSO worse.

paragraphs.heading: A name from Christmas
paragraphs.text: El Niño means "The Boy" in Spanish. Centuries ago, Peruvian fishermen called the event El Niño de Navidad, "The Christmas Boy", after the newborn Christ. An early recorded use of the name in a climate sense came in 1892, when Captain Camilo Carrillo told a geographical society congress in Lima about it. He reported that Peruvian sailors had named a warm current flowing south after the Christ Child, because it usually appeared around Christmas.
